EMPIRICAL RESEARCH PLAN  

===========================================================================  
1. Identification Strategy  
---------------------------------------------------------------------------  
Method: Difference-in-differences with continuous treatment intensity, implemented as an instrumental-variables (2SLS) “difference-in-differences-in-levels” design.

Idea  
• Gasoline price variation across Designated-Market-Areas (DMAs) and over months is plausibly exogenous to an individual’s vehicle choice once we saturate the regression with rich fixed effects.  
• The interaction of the local gasoline price with a vehicle’s ex-ante fuel-consumption requirement (Gallons per 10,000 miles = 10,000/MPG) generates exogenous, time-varying shocks to the expected discounted fuel cost of that vehicle relative to other models in the same market and month.  
• We ask: when the present value of lifetime fuel outlays for a model rises by $1, how much less are consumers willing to pay (or how much do model-level sales decline)? If the coefficient is –1, purchasers fully value fuel savings; if |coef|<1 they under-value them.

Formally (first stage)  
ExpectedFuelCost_{i,d,t} = γ · (GasPrice_{d,t} × GallonsPerMile_{i}) + controls + ε  

Second stage (value)  
log(Price)_{i,d,t} or Choice_{i,d,t} = β · Ĕ[FuelCost]_{i,d,t} + controls + u  

The IV absorbs all common shocks to vehicle demand and to regional gasoline prices, leaving only the interaction term as the instrument. This is a continuous DID because the gasoline-price shocks apply differentially to high- and low-MPG vehicles within a DMA-month.  

Why not RDD or a policy event study? 1999-2008 contains many small, continuous gasoline-price changes rather than a single sharp discontinuity; exploiting the full, rich variation yields more power and external validity.  

===========================================================================  
2. Treatment and Control  
---------------------------------------------------------------------------  
Treatment variable (continuous): Predicted discounted lifetime fuel expenditure of vehicle i for buyer in DMA d, month t:  

FuelCost_{i,d,t} = MilesYr × GasPrice_{d,t}/MPG_{i} × Σ_{s=1}^{T} δ^{s} × SurvivalProb_{i,s}  

where δ is a 4 % annual discount rate; MilesYr and SurvivalProb are from NHTSA.  

Instrument: GasPrice_{d,t} × (10,000/MPG_{i}).  

Control/comparison group: Models with higher MPG (hence lower treatment intensity) within the same market-month serve as the counterfactual for low-MPG models.  

Timing: Treatment intensity varies monthly; every DMA-month is both treated and control depending on the vehicle’s MPG.  

===========================================================================  
3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
---------------------------------------------------------------------------  
A1. Exogeneity of DMA-level gasoline-price movements.  
 • Plausible because short-run wholesale price changes are driven by world oil prices, refinery outages, state taxes, and transport costs rather than local vehicle-demand shocks.  

A2. Parallel trends across MPG groups absent gasoline-price changes.  
 • Conditional on DMA×month and model FE, the only systematic difference across MPG quartiles should be treatment.  

A3. No simultaneous un-controlled supply-side responses that target MPG groups differently.  
 • Dealer incentives or manufacturer rebates could react with lags; we include model×month FE in robustness checks.  

A4. Stable unit treatment value (SUTVA): one buyer’s treatment doesn’t spill over to another buyer’s choice set inside the same market-month once prices and inventories are controlled for.  

A5. First stage relevance: gas-price shocks significantly move expected fuel costs (trivially satisfied).  

===========================================================================  
4. Main Threats and Mitigations  
---------------------------------------------------------------------------  
T1. Endogenous model availability or promotions correlated with gasoline prices.  
 • Mitigation: Add model×month fixed effects in robustness; restrict to models continuously sold throughout the sample; control for manufacturer incentives if available.  

T2. Composition effects—different kinds of households buy cars when gas prices rise.  
 • Mitigation: Include census-block-group demographic controls interacted with month dummies; estimate within-buyer subsamples (e.g., repeat purchasers).  

T3. Measurement error in local gasoline prices.  
 • Mitigation: Aggregate OPIS station data to DMA-month using station weights; instrument reduces attenuation; show robustness to national price only and to bordering-state differentials.  

===========================================================================  
5. R Code Outline  
---------------------------------------------------------------------------  
```r
# 0. Packages -------------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)
library(fixest)      # fast fixed-effects + IV
library(modelsummary)

# 1. Load data ------------------------------------------------------------
trans  <- fread("transactions_1999_2008.csv")   # 2.96m rows
epa    <- fread("epa_fueleconomy.csv")          # MPG by model-year-trim
gas    <- fread("opis_dma_monthly_prices.csv")  # Price per gallon
surv   <- fread("nhtsa_survival_miles.csv")     # survival & miles

# 2. Merge & construct variables -----------------------------------------
# MPG
trans <- merge(trans, epa, by = c("make","model","model_year","trim"), all.x = TRUE)

# Gas price
trans[, ym := format(as.Date(date), "%Y-%m")]              # Year-month string
gas[, ym := sprintf("%d-%02d", year, month)]
trans <- merge(trans, gas[,.(dma, ym, gas_price)], by = c("dma","ym"), all.x = TRUE)

# Vehicle-specific gallons per mile
trans[, gpm := 1/comb_mpg]                                 # gallons per mile

# Present value of lifetime fuel cost (assume 11 years, 4% real r)
disc <- function(r,T) cumsum(cumprod(c(1, rep(1/(1+r),T-1))))[-1]
pv_weights <- disc(0.04, 11)                               # vector length 11
surv[, w := pv_weights[year]]                              # years 1-11
ann_miles <- 12000
surv_pv <- surv[, .(pv_miles = sum(miles * w)), by = "vehicle_class"]

trans <- merge(trans, surv_pv, by = "vehicle_class", all.x = TRUE)

trans[, fuel_cost := gas_price * pv_miles * gpm]

# 3. Main IV regression ---------------------------------------------------
# Equation: log(price) on fuel_cost IVed by gas_price * gpm
est_main <- feols(log(price) ~ 1 | dma^ym + model_id, 
                  iv = ~ fuel_cost | I(gas_price * gpm), 
                  data = trans, weights = ~quantity)

summary(est_main)

# 4. Robustness: add buyer demographics & DMA×trend -----------------------
est_rob <- feols(log(price) ~ income_q + race_share | dma^ym + model_id,
                 iv = ~ fuel_cost | I(gas_price * gpm),
                 data = trans)

modelsummary(list(Main = est_main, Demog = est_rob),
             gof_omit = 'Adj|AIC|BIC')

# 5. Event-study style check (graphical) ----------------------------------
# Bin gasoline price changes into deciles and plot implied β
```

===========================================================================  
6. Expected Results  
---------------------------------------------------------------------------  
Theory says a dollar increase in discounted fuel cost should lower the amount a purchaser is willing to pay by one dollar (β = −1) if buyers fully internalise lifetime fuel outlays.  
Empirical priors (e.g., Allcott & Wozny 2014) suggest β≈ −0.5 to −0.8. I therefore expect β ∈ [−0.4, −0.9]; point expectation ≈ −0.6, implying that on average car buyers discount future fuel expenses by roughly 40 %.  

===========================================================================  
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DiD/IV)  
---------------------------------------------------------------------------  
C1: Parallel trends of outcome across MPG groups pre-treatment ………………… 0.8  
C2: Exogenous assignment of gasoline-price shocks ………………………………………… 0.7  
C3: No time-varying composition or supply confounds …………………………………… 0.6  
C4: No spillovers/interference across units …………………………………………………… 0.9  
C5: Robust first-stage relevance & adequate power ……………………………………… 1.0  

Overall, while assumptions are plausible and testable, supply-side reactions and compositional changes remain the main caveats that must be probed extensively in robustness and falsification tests.
